ask: a rectangular board with mixed-number sides has a border of fractional width w on every side: the area of the border
chain: inner sides = each side minus 2w (a strip on BOTH sides) -> inner area as a product of mixed numbers -> border = outer area minus inner area
twist: the width comes off each side twice; perimeter x width (corners counted twice) and one-w-per-side are the natural errors

ask: g/h of a class are girls; p/q of the girls and r/s of the boys walk to school: the fraction of the whole class that walks
chain: girls who walk = g/h x p/q -> boys are 1 - g/h, boys who walk = (1 - g/h) x r/s -> add the two products over a common denominator
twist: each walking fraction is of a different part; using r/s of the class (or g/h for the boys too) is the natural error
q: of the girls & of the boys & fraction
e: of the girls|of the boys|fraction of the class

ask: Leo rounds each of four prices to the nearest whole dollar before adding; Mia adds the exact prices: how much greater is Leo's total than Mia's
chain: each price's rounding change (up is +, down is -) -> add the changes, letting ups and downs cancel (or: rounded total minus exact total) -> the difference
twist: rounding changes have directions that partly cancel; adding their sizes, or rounding the exact total once, are the natural errors

ask: a number pyramid of decimals (each brick is the sum of the two below it) with the top and two bottom bricks given: the missing middle bottom brick
chain: top = left + 2 x middle + right (the middle feeds both upper bricks) -> subtract the two outer bricks from the top -> halve
twist: the middle bottom brick is counted twice; top minus the two outer bricks without halving is the natural error

ask: a container that holds C (a mixed number) liters is f full: how many more liters fill it
chain: the empty part is 1 - f of the container -> (1 - f) x C as a product of fractions -> rename
twist: f is a fraction of the container, not an amount; C - f (subtracting the fraction as liters) is the natural error

ask: a jar full of honey weighs F kg; when it is f full it weighs W kg: the weight of the empty jar
chain: F - W is the honey in (1 - f) of the jar -> honey in a full jar = (F - W) / (1 - f) (for f = 1/2 double it) -> jar = F - full honey
twist: two readings of the same jar; the difference is a FRACTION of the contents, not all of it

ask: the product of two one-place decimals compared with the product of their nearest whole numbers: how far apart the two products are
chain: exact product a.b x c.d -> estimate (nearest whole x nearest whole) -> difference of the two products
twist: estimation error of a product is not the sum (or product) of the rounding changes

ask: a price with two decimal places is rounded to the nearest tenth of a dollar before n items are bought: how much more (or less) the rounded total is than the exact total
chain: rounding change of one price (to the nearest tenth) -> times n (the change happens on every item) -> the difference
twist: the rounding change repeats on every item; rounding the exact total once is the natural error

ask: two objects are measured with a ruler whose end is broken, so each object is laid between two marks that do not start at 0: their total length
chain: length of each = right mark - left mark (decimals) -> add the two lengths
twist: neither measurement starts at 0; reading the right marks only is the natural error

ask: a unit square has a vertical strip a wide and a horizontal strip b tall shaded (fractions): the area shaded by EXACTLY one strip
chain: overlap = a x b (fraction x fraction area) -> area covered at least once = a + b - ab -> exactly once = a + b - 2ab
twist: the overlap is removed twice: once because it is counted twice, once because it is shaded by both

ask: a full jar of nuts weighs F kg and the empty jar weighs J kg; nuts cost P dollars per kg: the cost of the nuts
chain: net weight = F - J -> cost = net weight x price per kg (decimal x decimal)
twist: the price applies to the contents only; multiplying the full weight is the natural error

ask: a unit square shaded with a vertical decimal strip and a horizontal decimal strip: the area left unshaded
chain: overlap = a x b -> covered = a + b - ab -> unshaded = 1 - covered
twist: the overlap must be subtracted once from the strip total; 1 - a - b (no overlap) and 1 - a - b - ab are the natural errors

ask: three houses at signed decimal positions on a straight road: the least possible total walking distance from one meeting point to all three
chain: total distance is least at the middle position -> add the distances from the middle point (= greatest - least)
twist: the best point is the median, not 0 or the mean; distances across 0 add

ask: four signed points on a number line (mixed numbers): the least possible total distance from one point to all four
chain: any point between the two middle points gives the least total -> total = (greatest - least) + (third - second)
twist: with four points the best place is a whole interval; distances across 0 add

ask: an account starts at a decimal balance; five deposits and withdrawals follow: the lowest balance at any time during the week
chain: running balance after each transaction (decimal add/subtract) -> compare the running balances -> the least
twist: the question is about an intermediate state, not the end; the final balance and start-minus-all-withdrawals are the natural errors

ask: a robot walks clockwise along the sides of a rectangle with signed decimal vertices, starting at the top-left vertex: the y-coordinate after it has walked d units
chain: top side length = difference of the x-coordinates across the y-axis -> the remaining distance goes down the right side -> y = top y minus the remaining distance
twist: the walk turns a corner, so the distance splits between two sides; ignoring the corner is the natural error

ask: a rope: u/v of it is used, then L meters more are used, and R meters are left: the original length
chain: undo the last step: R + L is what was left after the first use -> that is (1 - u/v) of the rope -> divide by 1 - u/v
twist: work backward in the reverse order; dividing by the USED fraction, or dividing first and adding L after, are the natural errors

ask: Ana divided a mixed number by a fraction by flipping the FIRST number instead of the divisor: by how much does her answer differ from the correct quotient
chain: correct quotient (multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor) -> her value (reciprocal of the dividend times the divisor) -> difference
twist: error analysis on fraction division: the misconception value must be computed

ask: a diver at a decimal depth below sea level descends a further fraction (u/v) of her current depth: her new elevation
chain: u/v of the depth (fraction x decimal) -> descend: subtract from the elevation -> new elevation (negative)
twist: the extra descent is a fraction of the depth, not an amount; subtracting u/v itself is the natural error
q: (below sea level) & (fraction|of the way|of its depth)

ask: q = a / b for two printed fractions; then q minus its reciprocal
chain: divide the fractions (multiply by the reciprocal) -> reciprocal of the quotient (= b / a) -> subtract
twist: the reverse quotient is the reciprocal of the first; recomputing it is the long way, and q + 1/q is the natural slip

ask: a hiker's signed elevation changes over five legs from a printed starting elevation: the highest elevation reached
chain: running elevation after each leg (signed decimal sums) -> compare -> the greatest
twist: an intermediate maximum, not the end; the final elevation and start-plus-all-climbs are the natural errors

ask: two houses on a road at signed positions; a store must be built so the total trip for k1 deliveries to one and k2 to the other is least: that least total
chain: weighted total distance is least at the house with more deliveries -> total = (fewer deliveries) x (distance between the houses)
twist: the best point is not the midpoint; the weights decide

ask: a meeting point P is chosen at a printed signed position: how much longer the total distance to three signed houses is than the least possible total
chain: total distance from P (three absolute distances, across 0) -> least total (from the middle house) -> subtract
twist: compares a given choice with the median optimum

ask: a recipe for m dozen (mixed number) uses c cups (mixed number): cups needed for n dozen
chain: cups per dozen = c / m (fraction division) -> times n
twist: scaling through a unit amount found by fraction division

ask: Ana estimates √n by placing n between the consecutive squares a^2 and (a+1)^2 and using the same fraction of the way from a to a+1: her estimate
chain: find the bracketing squares a^2 < n < (a+1)^2 -> fraction of the way = (n - a^2) / ((a+1)^2 - a^2) -> estimate = a + that fraction
twist: linear interpolation between perfect squares; the gap between consecutive squares is 2a + 1, not a or 10

ask: Ana estimates the cube root of n by placing n between consecutive cubes a^3 and (a+1)^3 and using the same fraction of the way from a to a+1: her estimate
chain: bracketing cubes a^3 < n < (a+1)^3 -> fraction of the way = (n - a^3) / ((a+1)^3 - a^3) -> estimate = a + that fraction
twist: interpolation between perfect cubes; the gap is (a+1)^3 - a^3

ask: two one-digit repeating decimals (0.aaa... + 0.bbb..., a + b > 9) are added: the exact sum as a fraction or mixed number
chain: each repeating decimal is a ninths fraction (a/9, b/9) -> add the ninths -> rename as a mixed number (or: column addition with a carry into EVERY repeating column)
twist: adding the repeats column by column needs the carry from the column to the right in every column; dropping it gives 1.111... instead of 1.222...

ask: two two-digit repeating decimals (0.abab... + 0.cdcd...) with a block sum above 99: the exact sum as a mixed number
chain: each is a ninety-ninths fraction -> add the 99ths -> rename past 1 (the extra 99/99 is the carry that wraps around the repeating block)
twist: the wrap-around carry: the block sum minus 99, not minus 100

ask: a one-digit repeating decimal minus a two-digit repeating decimal (0.aaa... - 0.bcbc...): the exact difference as a fraction
chain: 0.aaa... = 11a/99, 0.bcbc... = bc/99 -> subtract the 99ths -> lowest terms
twist: periods of different length must be written over the same 99

ask: x^2 = p/q and y^3 = -r/s for perfect-square and perfect-cube fractions: the least possible value of x + y
chain: two square roots (choose the negative one for the least sum) -> the cube root of the negative fraction (one value, negative) -> add the signed fractions
twist: 'least possible' forces the negative square root; the cube root has no choice

ask: x^3 = -p/q (a perfect cube fraction) and y^2 = r/s with y < 0: the value of x times y
chain: cube root of the negative fraction -> negative square root from the condition -> multiply (two negatives)
twist: two roots each with a sign decided differently, then the product sign rule

ask: using a printed fraction approximation of √7 (e.g. 2 13/20 ≈ 2.65), the approximate value of √28 + √63
chain: rewrite each radicand as a perfect square times 7 (28 = 4 x 7, 63 = 9 x 7) -> 2√7 + 3√7 = 5√7 -> multiply the approximation
twist: the roots combine only after the perfect-square factor is taken out; √(28 + 63) and halving instead of rooting are the natural errors

ask: a list of six numbers mixing perfect-square roots, a cube root, a repeating decimal and two irrationals: the sum of the rational numbers in the list
chain: classify each (perfect-square or perfect-cube root -> rational; repeating decimal -> rational, as a fraction; non-perfect root and pi -> irrational) -> convert the rationals to fractions -> add
twist: a repeating decimal is rational and must be converted; dropping it (or keeping a non-perfect root) is the natural error

ask: a total given as k x (a x 10^m) + (b x 10^n): the total in standard form
chain: multiply the count into the coefficient -> write both terms with the same power of 10 (or in standard form) -> add
twist: the two powers differ, so the coefficients cannot be added directly

ask: (a x 10^m) + (b x 10^n) with n = m - 1, written in scientific notation: its coefficient
chain: rewrite b x 10^n as (b/10) x 10^m -> add the coefficients -> renormalise if the coefficient passes 10
twist: the coefficient is only addable after matching powers

ask: (a x 10^-m) - (b x 10^-n) with n > m: the difference as a decimal in standard form
chain: write each in standard form with the right number of zeros -> line up places -> subtract
twist: negative exponents of different sizes; subtracting coefficients is the natural error

ask: 0.abab... is given as the fraction p/11 (or p/99); which fraction equals the decimal with the two digits of the block reversed
chain: 0.abab... + 0.baba... = 0.(a+b)(a+b)... -> when a + b = 9 the sum is 0.999... = 1 -> reversed = 1 - p/11 (or convert 0.baba... = ba/99 directly)
twist: the digit-reversal pair sums to a repeating 9s decimal

ask: Ana estimates √n by interpolating between consecutive squares; Ben uses the halfway value a + 1/2: how far apart the two estimates are
chain: bracketing squares -> interpolation fraction (n - a^2)/(2a + 1) -> difference from 1/2 over a common denominator
twist: compares two estimation methods; the fraction of the way must be found first

ask: a pyramid of decimals with four bottom bricks (each brick the sum of the two below): the top brick
chain: each middle bottom brick is used three times, each end brick once -> top = a + 3b + 3c + d (or build the three rows) -> add
twist: inner bricks feed several paths up; adding the bottom row once is the natural error

ask: three runners' segment times in mixed numbers of minutes for a relay; the team's planned total and the actual times: how far the actual total was over the plan
chain: add three mixed numbers with unlike denominators (twelfths) -> subtract the planned total -> regroup
twist: two totals compared; unlike denominators (fourths, sixths, thirds) must be renamed to twelfths

ask: three friends live at signed positions on a number line (fractions in twelfths): the least possible total distance from a meeting point, when the meeting point must be at one of the houses
chain: total from each house (sum of two distances, across 0) -> compare the three totals -> least (the middle house)
twist: comparing three totals of distances; the middle house wins

ask: Ana estimates √n for a mixed number n = a^2 + r/s by interpolating between consecutive squares: her estimate
chain: bracket the mixed number between a^2 and (a+1)^2 -> (n - a^2) / (2a + 1) as a fraction of a fraction -> add to a
twist: interpolation with a fractional numerator (complex fraction)

ask: five fractions with denominators 3, 4, 6 and 12 (one of them equal to 1/2): the sum of the ones GREATER than 1/2
chain: compare each fraction with the benchmark 1/2 (rename or compare numerator with half the denominator) -> keep those strictly greater -> add them over twelfths
twist: the fraction equal to 1/2 must be left out, and the sum of the kept ones is the answer, not their count

ask: S cups of flour (a mixed number) are used in servings of f cup (a fraction): how much MORE flour is needed to make one more full serving
chain: S / f by the reciprocal -> a whole number of servings and a fractional part of a serving -> the missing part (1 - fractional part) -> times f to get cups
twist: the leftover is read in servings and the shortfall must be converted back to cups

ask: a school's students are split into three grades by fractions; a different fraction of each grade rides the bus: the fraction of all the students who ride
chain: third grade's share = 1 - the other two -> each grade's riders = grade fraction x its riding fraction -> add the three products
twist: each riding fraction is of a different part; the third share must be found first

ask: a tank's water level starts at a mixed number of feet and changes by five rises and drops in mixed numbers with unlike denominators: the lowest level during the day
chain: running level after each change (unlike-denominator add/subtract, eighths) -> compare -> least
twist: the lowest point is an intermediate level, not the end; start-minus-all-drops and the final level are the natural errors

ask: a robot walks clockwise around a rectangle with signed decimal vertices starting at the bottom-left vertex: the x-coordinate after d units
chain: left side length = difference of the y-coordinates across the x-axis -> the remaining distance goes right along the top -> x = left x plus the remaining distance
twist: the walk turns a corner; ignoring it, or measuring a side across 0 by subtracting sizes, are the natural errors

ask: a list of decimals and roots (√0.25-type, √0.4-type, ∛0.008-type, a repeating decimal, π/10, a terminating decimal): the sum of the rational numbers as a fraction
chain: classify (root of a perfect-square decimal or perfect-cube decimal -> rational; repeating -> rational; non-perfect root, π multiple -> irrational) -> convert the rationals to fractions -> add
twist: a decimal inside a root can be a perfect square (0.25) or not (0.4); a repeating decimal is rational

ask: a list of roots of fractions, a cube root, a repeating decimal and two irrationals: the greatest rational number in the list minus the least rational number
chain: classify each as rational or irrational -> write the rationals as fractions -> order them -> greatest minus least
twist: the classification decides which numbers compete; a repeating decimal or a perfect-square root left out changes the extremes

ask: a list of five fractions, three of them perfect squares (one only after it is simplified, e.g. 18/50) and two not: the sum of the rational square roots
chain: simplify each fraction -> test numerator and denominator for perfect squares -> take the square roots of the perfect-square ones -> add
twist: a fraction can be a perfect square only after simplifying; leaving it out, or rooting numerators only, are the natural errors

ask: five powers with whole-number and fraction bases and zero or negative exponents: the sum of the ones whose value is less than 1
chain: evaluate each power (a negative exponent flips the base; a zero power is 1) -> keep the values less than 1 -> add them as fractions
twist: which powers count depends on evaluating them: a fraction base with a negative exponent is greater than 1, and a zero power is not less than 1
